FULL FAITH AND CREDIT FOR OUT-OF-STATE PROTECTIVE ORDERS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Morgan Casey

IDENTIFICATION OF THE OUT-OF-STATE PROTECTION ORDER
I, Jordan Lee, am the protected person under a protection order issued against Morgan Casey by Eighth Judicial District Court, Clark County, in Nevada, case/docket number D-26-123456, dated June 1, 2026 (including any later modification of that order). This document describes how California treats an order of this kind under California's Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act (Family Code section 6400 et seq.) and the related federal full faith and credit requirement (18 U.S.C. section 2265). It is informational only: it does not itself register, confirm, or enforce this order, and it does not determine whether this specific order in fact meets the statutory requirements described below -- that determination is made, case by case, by the California court or law enforcement officer asked to enforce it.

THE FULL FAITH AND CREDIT RULE FOR PROTECTIVE ORDERS
Federal law requires every state, Indian tribe, and U.S. territory to give full faith and credit to a protection order issued by another state, tribe, or territory that is consistent with the standard in 18 U.S.C. section 2265(b), and to enforce it as though it were the enforcing jurisdiction's own order. California implements that mandate through its own statute, the Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act: a person authorized under California law to enforce a protection order may seek enforcement of a valid foreign protection order in a California tribunal, and the tribunal must enforce its terms -- including relief a California tribunal would otherwise lack power to grant -- following California's own procedures for enforcing protection orders. For purposes of this California statute, a qualifying "protection order" is an injunction or other order issued under the domestic violence, family violence, or antistalking laws of the issuing state to prevent violent or threatening acts, harassment, contact, or physical proximity.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Any protection order issued that is consistent with subsection (b) of this section by the court of one State, Indian tribe, or territory (the issuing State, Indian tribe, or territory) shall be accorded full faith and credit by the court of another State, Indian tribe, or territory (the enforcing State, Indian tribe, or territory) and enforced by the court and law enforcement personnel of the other State, Indian tribal government or Territory"
  — 18 U.S.C. § 2265(a), the federal full faith and credit mandate (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2265)
  "A person authorized by the law of this state to seek enforcement of a protection order may seek enforcement of a valid foreign protection order in a tribunal of this state. The tribunal shall enforce the terms of the order, including terms that provide relief that a tribunal of this state would lack power to provide but for this section. The tribunal shall enforce the order, whether the order was obtained by independent action or in another proceeding, if it is an order issued in response to a complaint, petition, or motion filed by or on behalf of an individual seeking protection. In a proceeding to enforce a foreign protection order, the tribunal shall follow the procedures of this state for the enforcement of protection orders."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6402(a), California's own enforcement mandate for a valid foreign protection order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6402.)
  "“Protection order” means an injunction or other order, issued by a tribunal under the domestic violence, family violence, or antistalking laws of the issuing state, to prevent an individual from engaging in violent or threatening acts against, harassment of, contact or communication with, or physical proximity to, another individual."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6401(5), the statutory definition of a qualifying "protection order" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6401.)
  Known gap: This clause rests on two independent, separately enacted sources of law -- the federal full faith and credit statute, 18 U.S.C. section 2265(a), enacted as part of the Violence Against Women Act, and California's own Family Code section 6402(a), part of California's Uniform Interstate Enforcement of Domestic Violence Protection Orders Act -- so they corroborate rather than merely restate one another. The third citation, Family Code section 6401(5), is a different, independently numbered section from section 6402, so it is likewise not dependent on the section 6402 citation. This clause states that California's implementing statute reaches orders issued under the domestic violence, family violence, or antistalking laws of the issuing state; it does not resolve, for any specific out-of-state order, whether the issuing state actually classified that order under one of those bodies of law. The federal statute's own scope is broader on its face -- 18 U.S.C. section 2265(b) does not repeat the domestic-violence/family-violence/antistalking limitation found in the California statute's definitions -- and this clause does not attempt to reconcile that difference in scope between the two statutes; it states what each says.

CONDITIONS A FOREIGN ORDER MUST MEET: JURISDICTION AND NOTICE
Full faith and credit is not unconditional. Under the federal statute, a protection order is entitled to full faith and credit only if the issuing court had jurisdiction over the parties and the matter, and the respondent was given reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard sufficient to protect due process -- for an ex parte order, that notice and opportunity to be heard must come within the time required by the issuing jurisdiction's law, and in any event within a reasonable time after the order issued. California's own statute states essentially the same two conditions as part of its definition of a "valid" foreign protection order: the order must identify the protected individual and the respondent, be currently in effect, have been issued by a tribunal with jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter, and have been issued after the respondent received reasonable notice and an opportunity to be heard (or, for an ex parte order, notice and an opportunity to be heard within a reasonable time afterward). An order lacking any of these elements is not a "valid foreign protection order" for purposes of California's mandatory-enforcement statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "A protection order issued by a State, tribal, or territorial court is consistent with this subsection if— (1) such court has jurisdiction over the parties and matter under the law of such State, Indian tribe, or territory; and (2) reasonable notice and opportunity to be heard is given to the person against whom the order is sought sufficient to protect that person’s right to due process. In the case of ex parte orders, notice and opportunity to be heard must be provided within the time required by State, tribal, or territorial law, and in any event within a reasonable time after the order is issued, sufficient to protect the respondent’s due process rights."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 2265(b), the federal jurisdiction-and-notice standard for a qualifying protection order (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2265)
  "A foreign protection order is valid if it meets all of the following criteria: (1) Identifies the protected individual and the respondent. (2) Is currently in effect. (3) Was issued by a tribunal that had jurisdiction over the parties and subject matter under the law of the issuing state. (4) Was issued after the respondent was given reasonable notice and had an opportunity to be heard before the tribunal issued the order or, in the case of an order ex parte, the respondent was given notice and has had or will have an opportunity to be heard within a reasonable time after the order was issued, in a manner consistent with the rights of the respondent to due process."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6402(d), California's own criteria for a "valid" foreign protection order (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6402.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independent, separately enacted sources -- the federal statute, 18 U.S.C. section 2265(b), and California's own Family Code section 6402(d) -- rather than subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies. This clause states the statutory standard for validity; it does not, and cannot, determine whether any specific out-of-state order in fact satisfies these jurisdiction and notice requirements -- that is a fact-specific determination made by the enforcing court or officer, and (per the companion clause on this document) an order valid on its face is treated as prima facie evidence of its validity rather than as automatically, conclusively valid.

REGISTRATION IS NOT REQUIRED BEFORE CALIFORNIA MUST ENFORCE THE ORDER
Neither federal nor California law makes registering an out-of-state protection order in California a precondition to its enforcement here. The federal statute states directly that a qualifying order must be accorded full faith and credit notwithstanding a failure to comply with any requirement that it be registered or filed in the enforcing jurisdiction. California's own statute states the same rule for its enforcement mechanism: registration or filing of an order in California is not required for enforcement of a valid foreign protection order. A protected person does not need to register an out-of-state order with a California court before a California court or law enforcement officer is required to enforce it.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "Any protection order that is otherwise consistent with this section shall be accorded full faith and credit, notwithstanding failure to comply with any requirement that the order be registered or filed in the enforcing State, tribal, or territorial jurisdiction."
  — 18 U.S.C. § 2265(d)(2), no prior registration or filing required as a prerequisite for federal full faith and credit (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/18/2265)
  "Registration or filing of an order in this state is not required for the enforcement of a valid foreign protection order pursuant to this part."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6403(d), California's own statement that registration is not required for enforcement (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6403.)
  Known gap: This clause draws on two independent, separately enacted sources -- the federal statute, 18 U.S.C. section 2265(d)(2), and California's own Family Code section 6403(d) -- rather than subsections of a single section, so no single-section disclosure applies. This is likely the single most commonly misunderstood point in this area: many people assume an out-of-state order must first be registered in California before it can be enforced here, and that assumption is incorrect under both statutes quoted above. This clause does not address a separate, optional registration mechanism California provides for a protected person's own convenience, which is covered in a separate clause in this document and does not change the rule stated here.

A CALIFORNIA PEACE OFFICER'S DUTY TO ENFORCE A FACIALLY VALID ORDER
California's statute gives a California law enforcement officer a specific, checkable standard for enforcing an out-of-state protection order in the field. Once an officer determines there is probable cause to believe a valid foreign protection order exists and has been violated, the officer must enforce it as if it were a California order. Presenting an order that identifies both the protected individual and the respondent and appears, on its face, to be currently in effect is, by itself, enough to establish that probable cause -- an order stored electronically qualifies if it is retrievable in perceivable form, and a certified copy is not required. Separately, if an officer determines that an otherwise valid order cannot yet be enforced because the respondent has not been notified or served, the officer must inform the respondent of the order, make a reasonable effort to serve it, and give the respondent a reasonable opportunity to comply before enforcing it -- verbal notice of the order's terms is sufficient for this purpose.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "A law enforcement officer of this state, upon determining that there is probable cause to believe that a valid foreign protection order exists and that the order has been violated, shall enforce the order as if it were the order of a tribunal of this state. Presentation of a protection order that identifies both the protected individual and the respondent and, on its face, is currently in effect constitutes, in and of itself, probable cause to believe that a valid foreign protection order exists. For the purposes of this section, the protection order may be inscribed on a tangible medium or may have been stored in an electronic or other medium if it is retrievable in perceivable form. Presentation of a certified copy of a protection order is not required for enforcement."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6403(a), the probable-cause standard for enforcement and what constitutes probable cause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6403.)
  "If a law enforcement officer of this state determines that an otherwise valid foreign protection order cannot be enforced because the respondent has not been notified or served with the order, the officer shall inform the respondent of the order, make a reasonable effort to serve the order upon the respondent, and allow the respondent a reasonable opportunity to comply with the order before enforcing the order. Verbal notice of the terms of the order is sufficient notice for the purposes of this section."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6403(c), the notice-and-opportunity-to-comply procedure when the respondent has not yet been served (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6403.)
  Known gap: Family Code section 6403, subdivisions (a) and (c), quoted here, are both provisions of a single California statutory section -- not independent of one another. This clause does not restate subdivision (b), which separately allows an officer to consider other information toward probable cause when no order is presented, or the officer's civil immunity for a good-faith arrest under a facially regular order, which is addressed by a different, independently numbered section (Family Code section 6405) not covered in this document. This is one state's statute, describing how California specifically implements the federal full faith and credit mandate for its own peace officers; it is not a claim about how any other state's officers are instructed to handle an out-of-state protection order.

AN OPTIONAL REGISTRATION MECHANISM, FOR THE PROTECTED PERSON'S CONVENIENCE
Separately from the no-registration-required enforcement rule described elsewhere in this document, California's statute gives a protected person the option to register an out-of-state protection order with a California court so that it is entered into the California Restraining and Protective Order System. Registration under this mechanism is initiated upon the request of the person in possession of the order -- the statute's implementing rules describe this as a process by which that person "may voluntarily register" the order. A registered order's record is sealed, with access limited to law enforcement, the person who registered it (upon written request with proof of identification), the defense after arraignment on a criminal charge involving an alleged violation, or by further court order. No fee may be charged for this registration, and the court clerk must provide the required Judicial Council forms free of charge.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-05]
  "A foreign protection order shall, upon request of the person in possession of the order, be registered with a court of this state in order to be entered in the California Restraining and Protective Order System established under Section 6380. The Judicial Council shall adopt rules of court to do the following: (1) Set forth the process whereby a person in possession of a foreign protection order may voluntarily register the order with a court of this state for entry into the California Restraining and Protective Order System. (2) Require the sealing of foreign protection orders and provide access only to law enforcement, the person who registered the order upon written request with proof of identification, the defense after arraignment on criminal charges involving an alleged violation of the order, or upon further order of the court. (b) A fee shall not be charged for the registration of a foreign protection order. The court clerk shall provide all Judicial Council forms required by this part to a person in possession of a foreign protection order free of charge."
  — Cal. Fam. Code § 6404(a)-(b), the optional, voluntary registration mechanism and its sealing and no-fee provisions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=FAM&sectionNum=6404.)
  Known gap: This is a single statutory section (Family Code section 6404, subdivisions (a)-(b), quoted here as one contiguous passage); no additional independent source was found for this specific optional mechanism. This clause should not be read to imply that registration is required for enforcement -- the immediately preceding point in this document (Family Code section 6403(d) and 18 U.S.C. section 2265(d)(2)) states the opposite: enforcement does not depend on registration. This mechanism exists for a protected person's own convenience -- for example, so that the order appears in a statewide law enforcement system -- not as a gatekeeping step. This clause does not describe the Judicial Council rules of court adopted to implement this section in further procedural detail beyond what the statute itself states.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT AND SIGNATURE
I declare under penalty of perjury under the laws of the State of California that the foregoing is true and correct to the best of my knowledge. Executed on September 5, 2026, at Sacramento, California.
